details.label: Summary
details.text: Damaging wind and large hail threat continues within WW576 and WW578

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A cluster of supercells continue southeastward across southwestern South Dakota. These have produced hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter and damaging wind up to 87 mph. These will likely continue to pose a risk for large hail and damaging wind downstream over the next few hours, given the very favorably unstable and deeply sheared environment across western Nebraska, where MLCAPE around 1000-2400 J/kg and deep layer shear around 45-50 kts is depicted by SPC Mesoanalyis. Trends in hi-res guidance suggest that this cluster may eventually interact with convection coming out of Colorado later this evening, with a continued damaging wind risk through the evening

details.label: Summary
details.text: Severe thunderstorms will continue to pose a severe wind and hail threat for the next hour or two, but should become increasingly sporadic through the evening hours. Downstream watch issuance will most likely not be required

details.label: Discussion
details.text: The remnants of an MCS continue to push southward across the lower OH Valley, and although storm mode has become increasingly disorganized and outflow-dominant (likely a consequence of diminishing deep-layer wind shear with southward extent), lightning counts have increased over the past 20 minutes within a few cells from eastern MO into far southwest IN. This uptick in intensity comes as convection begins to push into a regional buoyancy maximum where MLCAPE was recently analyzed to be around 3500 J/kg. Consequently, the potential for large hail (most likely around one inch) and strong/severe downburst winds should linger for the next 1-2 hours as convection migrates through the best thermodynamic environment. However, regional reflectivity/velocity imagery shows that much of this activity is quickly becoming displaced behind a coherent convective outflow and/or has storm motions into the cold pool. Weaker deep-layer wind shear with southward extent should maintain the outflow-dominant nature of the convection and will eventually promote storm weakening and an increasingly isolated severe threat heading into the mid/late evening. Latest HRRR/RRFS time-lagged guidance captures this trend well and suggests the severe threat may not extend much beyond the southern bounds of WW 577. While convective trends will continue to be monitored as storms push through the buoyancy maximum, downstream watch issuance is currently not anticipated
